## Scope

The memory contract owns **where bytes come from, who is charged for them, and what
happens when there are no more** — everywhere except the value encodings themselves.
Concretely:

* **The allocation substrate.** One jemalloc arena per shard thread, bound once at thread
  start — and a bind the allocator refuses is **fatal at boot**, not a shard that runs
  unattributed: a shard without an arena decides with nothing measuring its core, and there
  is no configuration that lets it serve anyway. A shard legitimately has no arena only
  where there are no arenas to bind at all — the simulation seam, or a build whose allocator
  has none — which is a configuration rather than a failure. Also here: the shard-placement
  seam that decides whether a shard is an OS thread or a task on the simulation's one
  thread; and the `mallctl` reads that turn allocator state into numbers — the process-wide
  chokepoint behind `INFO memory`, `MEMORY PURGE` and the `frogdb_allocator_*` gauges
  (`frogdb-server/crates/telemetry/src/jemalloc.rs`), and the per-shard reads layered on it
  (`shard_arenas.rs`, [FM-MEMORY-008](#fm-memory-008--a-shards-arena-figure-is-that-shards-own-bytes-says-so-before-it-is-taken-and-is-never-read-on-a-shard-core)).
* **The broker and its budgets.** The per-core memory broker, the `Budget` handle a
  non-keyspace subsystem holds, and the charge/release calls at that subsystem's growth
  seam. Seven subsystems are declared; four hold a live budget today — `network_output`
  ([FM-MEMORY-002](#fm-memory-002--buffered-reply-bytes-are-charged-to-a-per-core-networkoutput-budget-and-released-when-they-drain)),
  `client_tracking`, `txn_buffering`
  ([txn.md FM-TXN-054](/specifications/txn/#fm-txn-054--a-multi-that-outgrows-the-transaction-buffer-is-poisoned-at-queue-time))
  and `persistence`. `replication_backlog`, `wal_channel` and `fullsync_staging` are named
  in the breakdown and charged by nobody yet; see [Open items](#open-items).
* **The refusal and reclamation verdicts.** What `maxmemory` is measured against, which
  writes are refused when it is exceeded, what eviction selects and what it guarantees
  about what it did not select, and that the pass terminates
  ([FM-MEMORY-004](#fm-memory-004--eviction-runs-only-under-the-maxmemory-verdict-and-a-write-is-refused-only-after-the-policy-has-been-given-its-chances)
  through [FM-MEMORY-007](#fm-memory-007--eviction-frees-a-key-or-reports-that-it-cannot-it-never-spins)).
* **What a retained byte may alias.** The zero-copy parse path hands commands slices of the
  connection's pooled read buffer; this spec owns where a copy is taken so that buffer can
  be recycled
  ([FM-MEMORY-003](#fm-memory-003--nothing-retained-past-a-commands-completion-aliases-the-connections-pooled-read-buffer)).

Out of scope, owned elsewhere: the *layout* of a value (the keyspace table and its
encodings are a correctness contract of their own, not a memory one, and get their own
spec when they land); durability ordering ([persistence.md](/specifications/persistence/)); what a
replication link puts on the wire ([replication.md](/specifications/replication/)); slot ownership
([cluster.md](/specifications/cluster/)). Rows here stop at what an operator or a client can observe:
a refusal, an eviction, a shed connection, a metric, or a process that stayed inside its
configured ceiling.

## Invariant vocabulary

These are the nouns every row uses. They are defined once here so no row has to
re-explain them and no two rows can mean different things by the same word.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Budget** | A handle, held by exactly one subsystem on exactly one core, carrying a limit and a current charge. It is the only thing that can authorize growth of a non-keyspace buffer. A `Budget` is not a counter a subsystem updates after the fact — the charge is the permission, taken *before* the bytes exist. |
| **broker** | The per-core owner of every `Budget` on that core, and the one component that reads allocator truth for the core. It arbitrates between subsystems (whose limits may sum to more than the core's share) and publishes the per-subsystem breakdown an operator reads. One broker per core; brokers do not share state, consistent with the shared-nothing topology (PRD R3). |
| **arena** | A jemalloc arena, one per shard thread, bound once at thread start via `arenas.create` + `thread.arena`. The arena is the *attribution* mechanism: bytes allocated by a shard thread are that shard's bytes, and no other shard's arena reports them. It is not an isolation boundary the code can rely on for safety — nothing stops a pointer crossing threads — which is why the no-cross-core-refcount rule (PRD R3) is a separate invariant rather than a consequence of arenas. |
| **charge** | The act of asking a `Budget` for `n` bytes and being told yes or no, before allocating them. A charge that succeeds is held until the matching release; a charge that fails is a refusal the caller must handle at that seam — never a charge taken anyway with a warning logged. |
| **shed** | The response to a failed charge when the growth belongs to a client the server may drop: the connection is closed, or its buffered output is discarded, and the server keeps running. Redis's `client-output-buffer-limit` classes are shed policy. Shedding is *observable* — it produces a metric and a log line naming the class — because a silently shed client is indistinguishable from a network fault. |
| **backpressure** | The response to a failed charge when the producer can be made to wait instead: the write is not accepted, the reader is not polled, the channel blocks. Backpressure preserves the work; shedding discards it. Every buffer must state which of the two it does, and no buffer may do neither. |
| **ceiling** vs **budget** | A **ceiling** is a constant bound on one quantity, checked at one site, that exists to make an absurd value fail cleanly — a wire-supplied length that cannot be a real dataset. A **budget** is a live allowance derived from what this node actually has, shared between competing consumers, that can refuse a perfectly reasonable request because the node is full. A ceiling defends against a lie; a budget defends against the truth. The two are not substitutes, and a row must not claim a ceiling gives it a budget's guarantee. |
| **accounted contents** | `Store::memory_used()`: the shard's running sum of `Entry::memory_size()`. Exact with respect to what the keyspace accounts for, and deliberately *run-stable* — a block-backed value excludes its `Vec`/`VecDeque` spare capacity so the same contents report the same figure whatever churn built them. It is therefore not a footprint: allocator overhead is outside it, and a freshly doubled buffer can hold about twice what it reports. This is the figure the `maxmemory` verdict binds to. |

## FM-MEMORY-001 — a connection past its `client-output-buffer-limit` class is disconnected and its buffered output released

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger | A connection whose queued reply bytes reach the hard limit of its class, or stay at or above the soft limit continuously for `soft-seconds`. The class is the connection's role at the moment of the judgement: `replica` if it has announced a replica listening port, else `pubsub` if it holds a subscription channel, else `normal`. Limits come from `server.client-output-buffer-limit`, spelled as Redis spells it (`<class> <hard> <soft> <soft-seconds>`, repeated per class, `slave` an alias for `replica`, Redis's size suffixes and Redis's defaults `normal 0 0 0`, `replica 256mb 64mb 60`, `pubsub 32mb 8mb 60`; `0` disables a limit). |
| Observable | The connection is torn down rather than served — the client sees a close or a reset, never the reply that exceeded the allowance. Its buffered bytes are discarded and released from `Subsystem::NetworkOutput` before the error propagates, so a shed connection costs the shard nothing after the verdict. `frogdb_client_output_buffer_disconnects_total{class,reason}` counts it, with `reason` distinguishing `hard_limit`, `soft_limit` and `budget_refused`, and a `warn` log names class, reason and byte count. A connection whose output stays inside its class's allowance is served in full. |
| NOT observable | A limit applied to a class the operator did not configure — an unnamed class keeps its Redis default rather than inheriting another class's number. A malformed `client-output-buffer-limit` silently replaced by the default: the parse refuses the boot, because a limit the operator believes they set and does not have is worse than none. A shed connection whose bytes stay charged (the pre-fix behavior wrote the condemned buffer out on the way to the error). Also not observable: the soft window forced end to end — the reply path applies backpressure at the codec's boundary rather than accumulating, and a connection whose client has stopped reading is parked inside its write, so the window is forced at the housekeeping-tick seam that judges an idle connection rather than over a socket. Also not observable: a gap at the `PSYNC` handoff. The `replica` class does not stop at the edge of the client connection — the account, and the charge in it, are carried into the replication feed, which keeps reporting against them until the link ends ([replication.md FM-REPLICATION-069](/specifications/replication/#fm-replication-069--the-replica-feed-is-charged-to-networkoutput-and-judged-against-the-replica-output-buffer-class)). What that row owns is *which* feed bytes are reported and what a shed verdict does to the link; what this row owns is the class, its limits and the budget they are charged to, and both sides use this one implementation. |
| Invariant | One seam decides. `OutputBufferAccount::judge` is the only place a class limit is compared against buffered bytes, `frame_io::account_buffered_output` is the only caller that measures them (codec write buffer + `resp3_buf` + the pub/sub delivery queue, both protocol versions), reached from the write path and from the connection's one-second housekeeping tick so an idle connection is still judged, and `frame_io::shed_output` is the only exit — it clears both buffers, releases the charge, emits the metric and returns the error. The pub/sub overflow path was migrated onto that exit rather than keeping its own disconnect. After a `PSYNC` handoff the measuring caller and the exit are the feed's, not the connection's (`ReplicaFeedAccount`, [replication.md FM-REPLICATION-069](/specifications/replication/#fm-replication-069--the-replica-feed-is-charged-to-networkoutput-and-judged-against-the-replica-output-buffer-class)), but `judge` is still the only comparison. `OutputVerdict` is `#[must_use]`, so a caller cannot take a verdict and ignore it. |
| Outcome variant | `OutputVerdict::{Keep, Shed(ShedReason)}` / `ShedReason::{HardLimit, SoftLimit, BudgetRefused}` |
| Forced by | `the_hard_limit_sheds_at_once`, `the_soft_limit_sheds_only_after_the_window`, `dropping_under_the_soft_limit_restarts_the_window`, `changing_class_restarts_the_soft_window_and_switches_the_limit`, `test_normal_class_hard_limit_disconnects_an_oversized_reply`, `test_a_pipeline_within_the_limit_is_served_in_full`, `test_slow_subscriber_output_buffer_bound_disconnects`, `the_idle_tick_sheds_a_connection_that_stays_above_the_soft_mark`, `test_a_malformed_limit_spec_is_a_configuration_error` |
| Bug refs | [memory-architecture issue 18](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/done/18-network-buffer-pools-and-output-limits.md) |

## FM-MEMORY-002 — buffered reply bytes are charged to a per-core `NetworkOutput` budget and released when they drain

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Any reply buffered for a client, on either protocol version, and any drain of that buffer. |
| Observable | The shard broker publishes a `NetworkOutput` row: `frogdb_memory_budget_limit_bytes{shard,subsystem="network_output"}` carries the per-core ceiling, and the per-subsystem breakdown carries what is currently held. Charged bytes track the buffer exactly — a connection's charge is the delta against what it already held, and a drain releases every byte it was holding. A budget that refuses a charge sheds the connection with `ShedReason::BudgetRefused` (FM-MEMORY-001's exit), rather than the bytes being buffered anyway. |
| NOT observable | A budget shared between cores — the handle is thread-local, so a charge on one shard thread is invisible to another and no cross-core atomic is taken on the reply path. (The *feed* path is not the reply path: an account that crosses the `PSYNC` handoff keeps the `Budget` the connection opened it on — an `Arc` over atomics — and is then reported to from the feed's own tasks, which is a cross-thread charge onto one core's budget by construction. See [replication.md FM-REPLICATION-069](/specifications/replication/#fm-replication-069--the-replica-feed-is-charged-to-networkoutput-and-judged-against-the-replica-output-buffer-class).) A charge that outlives its bytes: repeated accounting of the same buffer sets the charge rather than adding to it, so a connection cannot inflate the subsystem by being measured twice. A nonzero steady-state `charged_bytes` in a healthy sample is also not promised — the write path drains a batch before returning, so the observable that pins adoption is the published row and its limit, not a sampled charge. Also not observable: a subsystem label or a refusal message that drifts. The seven `Subsystem` strings and the two `Disposition` strings are the operator-facing names in metric labels, `INFO` fields and log lines, and changing one is a break rather than a rename. |
| Invariant | `frogdb_memory::network_output` owns one `Budget` per core in a `thread_local!`, opened against `Subsystem::NetworkOutput` on the shard's own thread; `OutputBufferAccount` holds the single `Charge` for a connection and `set_buffered`/`release_all` are the only mutations of it — a flush re-measures through `set_buffered` rather than claiming a drain, so bytes still queued for the client keep their soft window running. A connection that completes `PSYNC` moves that same account into its replication feed rather than releasing and reopening one, so the charge stays on the core that opened it and no replica-bound byte is uncharged at the handoff ([replication.md FM-REPLICATION-069](/specifications/replication/#fm-replication-069--the-replica-feed-is-charged-to-networkoutput-and-judged-against-the-replica-output-buffer-class)). A budget the broker did not mint is *adopted* rather than re-opened, so a process-wide allowance (RocksDB's, opened once at `RocksStore::open`) is reported by exactly one core under its own subsystem and never minted a second time. |
| Outcome variant | `Charge` / `OutputVerdict::Shed(ShedReason::BudgetRefused)` |
| Forced by | `buffered_bytes_are_charged_to_the_network_output_budget`, `a_refused_charge_sheds_the_connection`, `draining_releases_every_charged_byte`, `a_core_has_one_budget`, `budgets_do_not_cross_cores`, `test_network_output_budget_is_published_for_resp2_and_resp3`, `a_shed_connection_releases_its_charge`, `the_per_core_ceiling_is_the_documented_size`, `the_default_limits_are_the_documented_sizes`, `subsystem_and_disposition_labels_are_the_operator_facing_names`, `a_refusal_message_names_the_subsystem_the_bytes_and_the_disposition`, `available_counts_down_as_the_budget_fills`, `available_is_zero_rather_than_negative_when_the_limit_drops_below_the_charge`, `adopting_reports_an_existing_pool_without_minting_a_second_one`, `adopting_files_the_pool_under_the_budgets_own_subsystem`, `adopting_does_not_replay_refusals_taken_before_the_broker_saw_the_pool` |

## FM-MEMORY-003 — nothing retained past a command's completion aliases the connection's pooled read buffer

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger | A command parsed on the zero-copy path — its name and arguments are refcounted slices of the connection's pooled read buffer ([PRD](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/PRD.md) R12) — whose bytes would be retained past the command's completion: a value installed into the keyspace, a blocking op parked on a shard, or a command hopped to a foreign core. (A scatter participant's per-op key batch is not one of these: it lives only for the one synchronous round trip.) |
| Observable | The retained copy is made exactly at the escape point, so the read buffer's allocation is releasable the moment the command's own slices drop: a `SET` leaves the source buffer unshared while the key stays stored, a parked `BLMOVE`/`XREADGROUP` holds no slice of it, a command hopped to a foreign core carries no slice of it, and a partitioned multi-key command's per-shard batches are still slices of it (one synchronous round trip; the shard's install seam makes the one copy of whatever it retains). The pool observes the discipline directly — a read buffer handed back (`recycle` on the idle tick, `release` at close) with every slice dropped parks for reuse; one handed back with a slice still live is freed to the slice rather than parked. Between hops, batching holds: keys spanning K shards cost K lock-request messages, not one per key (`frogdb_scatter_gather_shards` records K). |
| NOT observable | A stored value or parked op whose bytes still alias the read buffer past the command's completion — the next lease of that buffer would overwrite data the keyspace can still read, so no test may ever observe a `Bytes` retained past the round trip sharing the source allocation. A buffer pinned indefinitely by a retained slice: ten thousand stored keys must not hold ten thousand read buffers alive. A copy paid where nothing escapes — bytes already uniquely owned (replication apply, recovery) pass through `detach_bytes` unchanged. |
| Invariant | One helper decides: `frogdb_protocol::detach_bytes` copies iff the `Bytes` still shares its allocation (`is_unique`), and every escape point calls it — the keyspace install seam (`HashMapStore::install`, which also calls `Value::detach_network_aliases`), the blocking-park boundary (`detach_wait_inputs`, `BlockingOp::detach`), the foreign-core hop (`command_for_shard` → `ParsedCommand::detached`), the connection-local retention points (MULTI queue, WATCH set, tracking prefixes, client name and library info), the cross-connection ones (slow log — always a copy, its entries outlive the command on shard 0 — pub/sub publish, script cache), and the collection-internal ones (quicklist plain nodes, stream group/consumer/PEL names, vector-set element names, time-series compaction destinations). Scatter partitioning (`partition_keys`, MSET pairs) is deliberately *not* an escape point: the batches are per-op slices and the shard's install seam copies once. `detach_bytes` decides by `is_unique`, which is sound only because the socket is polled between commands — the one mid-command read-ahead (draining pipelined frames while a blocking command parks) copies each frame out via `detach_frame` before the next poll. A `reserve` during that read-ahead can still move the codec onto a fresh allocation and leave the parked command's own args holding the old one; that never pins it behind a short key because a `ParsedCommand` holds its name and every arg as slices of one allocation (so none is unique while the command is alive) and after the wait those args are only borrowed (the slow log copies, the hot-key sampler takes `&[u8]`), never moved into a retention point. The pool side is `BytesMut::try_reclaim` in `BufferPool::give`: a shared buffer is never parked; the read buffer itself is pool-seeded at accept (`lease`) and returned through `recycle`/`release`. |
| Outcome variant | `detach_bytes` (copy) / pass-through (already unique) / `PoolStats::freed_returns` (lease dropped while shared) |
| Forced by | `test_detach_bytes_copies_only_when_shared`, `test_detach_frame_releases_source_buffer`, `test_command_detach_releases_source_buffer`, `queued_commands_and_watches_detach_from_the_shared_read_buffer`, `install_detaches_args_that_alias_a_shared_read_buffer`, `blocking_op_detach_releases_the_shared_read_buffer`, `wait_inputs_detach_from_the_shared_read_buffer`, `read_ahead_realloc_leaves_parked_args_shared_and_parked_frames_detached`, `foreign_shard_hop_detaches_the_command_from_the_read_buffer`, `local_shard_keeps_the_zero_copy_command`, `tracking_prefixes_detach_from_the_shared_read_buffer`, `truncate_args_copies_a_slice_that_is_the_sole_holder_of_its_buffer`, `partition_batches_keys_per_shard_without_copying`, `mset_partition_sends_read_buffer_slices`, `a_shared_slice_keeps_the_lease_out_of_the_pool_until_it_drops`, `a_pipelined_burst_of_slices_releases_the_lease_only_when_the_last_drops`, `a_scatter_over_k_shards_sends_exactly_k_lock_messages` |
| Bug refs | [memory-architecture issue 19](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/open/19-zero-copy-parse-path.md) |

## FM-MEMORY-004 — eviction runs only under the `maxmemory` verdict, and a write is refused only after the policy has been given its chances

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger | A write arriving at a shard whose accounted contents exceed its share of `maxmemory`, under a policy other than `noeviction`. Also its negative: the same write arriving while the shard is inside its limit, or with no limit configured. |
| Observable | Inside the limit, nothing is evicted and nothing is sampled — a `SET` under an unreached `maxmemory` leaves every other key present and the eviction counters at zero. Over it, the write is served if the policy can free enough, and refused with `-OOM` only after the pass has run: up to ten victims are taken and the limit re-measured between each. `noeviction` refuses without taking a victim. A refusal counts `frogdb_eviction_oom_total{shard}` and logs at `warn`; a *sample* of the same state (`sample_oom_state`, the script-start admission's probe) does neither, so asking the question cannot inflate the counter. |
| NOT observable | Eviction as a background activity: nothing in the server evicts on a timer, on read pressure, or on a policy change — the verdict is the only trigger, so a shard inside its limit has exactly the keys it was given. A refusal taken before the policy has run. A write refused because *another* shard is over its limit: the limit, the measurement and the victim are all one shard's (PRD R3). Also not observable: a verdict taken against the process's footprint. The figure compared to the limit is the shard's **accounted contents** (`Store::memory_used()`), not RSS, not the allocator's process-wide gauges, and not the per-shard arena sample [FM-MEMORY-008](#fm-memory-008--a-shards-arena-figure-is-that-shards-own-bytes-says-so-before-it-is-taken-and-is-never-read-on-a-shard-core) publishes. So a shard is never refused because its allocator is fragmented or because a neighbour's arena grew — and, in the other direction, the true footprint can exceed the figure the verdict binds to (spare capacity in a value's buffers is excluded for run-stability, worst case about 2× for a freshly doubled buffer). Because that figure is exact rather than sampled, the boundary is exact too: sitting at the limit is inside it, and a `maxmemory` of `0` is "no limit" rather than a limit of zero. |
| Invariant | `ShardWorker::check_memory_for_write_inner` is the only eviction driver: one loop, bounded at ten attempts, entered only when `is_over_memory_limit` is true, and `evict_one` is reachable from nowhere else. `is_over_memory_limit` is the only comparison — `store.memory_used() > eviction.memory_limit()`, short-circuiting on a zero limit before it reads anything — and `ShardEviction::update_config` is the only writer of that limit, dividing the configured node-wide `maxmemory` by the shard count so each shard defends its own share. `check_memory_for_write` (`rejecting = true`) and `sample_oom_state` (`rejecting = false`) share that body and differ only in whether `oom_verdict` logs and counts. Adding a keyspace backend with its own cold ordering did not add a second gate: `Store::eviction_candidates` is consulted *inside* `evict_one`, through `choose_victim`. |
| Outcome variant | `Ok(())` (freed enough) / `CommandError::OutOfMemory` (`EvictionOomTotal`) |
| Forced by | `nothing_is_evicted_while_the_shard_is_inside_its_limit`, `a_write_over_the_limit_evicts_before_it_is_served`, `noeviction_refuses_the_write_without_taking_a_victim`, `sampling_the_oom_state_does_not_count_a_refusal`, `the_verdict_binds_to_the_accounted_contents_at_an_exact_boundary` |
| Bug refs | — |

## FM-MEMORY-005 — eviction never takes a key outside the configured policy's candidate set

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger | An eviction pass under a `volatile-*` policy against a keyspace holding both TTL'd and persistent keys, or under any policy against a keyspace holding warm (already spilled) entries. |
| Observable | A `volatile-*` policy evicts only keys carrying a TTL: a keyspace of persistent keys under `volatile-lru` frees nothing and the write is refused with `-OOM` rather than a persistent key being taken. Confinement is per *key*, not per storage unit — on the segmented backend a segment mixing TTL'd and persistent keys yields its TTL'd keys and keeps the rest, so the granularity of the *ordering* (a segment) is never the granularity of the *decision* (a key). Warm entries are never nominated: they hold no hot bytes, so evicting one would free nothing. |
| NOT observable | A persistent key evicted under any `volatile-*` policy, for any backend, at any pressure. A cold ordering overriding the candidate set: a backend that nominates is asked with the policy's predicate and its answer is taken as final, so an empty nomination becomes the OOM verdict rather than falling through to a sampling pass that would ignore the confinement. Also not observable here: *which* eligible key is chosen — that is the policy's ranking, and the two backends rank differently by construction (sampled recency/frequency vs. 2Q over segments). This row owns the set, not the order within it. |
| Invariant | `ShardWorker::choose_victim` is the only place a victim is named, for both the delete and the spill path, so a tiered policy spills exactly the key a non-tiered one would delete. It asks `Store::eviction_candidates` only for policies whose `EvictionPolicy::candidate_source` is `CandidateSource::Cold` (the recency and frequency ones; `*-random` and `volatile-ttl` are ordered by something a cold list does not encode), and `HashMapStore::eviction_candidates` supplies the eligibility predicate — `entry.is_hot() && (!volatile_only \|\| entry.metadata.expires_at.is_some())` — rather than the container, which knows nothing of TTLs. The sampling path's confinement is unchanged and unshared: `sample_volatile_keys` draws from the expiry index, which holds only volatile keys. |
| Outcome variant | `Option<Vec<Bytes>>` — `None` (no cold ordering, sample instead) / `Some(vec![])` (ordering exists, candidate set empty → OOM) / `Some(keys)` |
| Forced by | `a_volatile_policy_never_evicts_a_persistent_key`, `only_recency_and_frequency_policies_ask_for_a_cold_ordering`, `confinement_nominates_only_what_the_policy_may_take`, `a_single_call_never_nominates_a_key_twice` |
| Bug refs | [memory-architecture issue 12](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/done/12-segment-2q-eviction.md) |

## FM-MEMORY-006 — every eviction is observable: an `evicted` notification, the eviction counters, and a replicated removal

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger | A key removed by the eviction pass, and — as the contrasting variant — a value moved to the warm tier by a tiered policy. |
| Observable | A true eviction fires the `evicted` keyspace notification, counts `frogdb_eviction_keys_total{shard,policy}` and `frogdb_eviction_bytes_total{shard,policy}` by the bytes the key actually held, bumps the key's WATCH version, writes the removal to the WAL and replicates it as a synthetic `DEL`, so a replica and a restarted node agree the key is gone. A spill fires **no** `evicted` event and bumps no version — the key is still readable and unspills on next access — and is observable instead through `frogdb_tiered_spills_total` / `frogdb_tiered_bytes_spilled_total`. Sampling is counted separately (`frogdb_eviction_samples_total`), so a backend that nominates from a cold ordering instead of sampling is visible as sampling that stops rather than as evictions that stop. |
| NOT observable | An eviction the rest of the system does not learn about: no path removes a key for memory pressure without the notification, the counters and the replicated removal, whichever backend chose it. An `evicted` event for a spill, or a WATCH invalidated by one. A byte count taken from an estimate rather than from the entry: the freed figure is the key's own **accounted contents** (`memory_size`), read before the removal — the same figure the verdict in FM-MEMORY-004 binds to, so what the counter reports and what the limit measures cannot drift apart. |
| Invariant | `ShardWorker::delete_for_eviction` is the only removal-for-memory path, and it reaches `run_internal_removal_effects` with `RemovalReason::Evicted`, which is what owns the notification, the WAL record and the replication. `spill_for_eviction` deliberately does not route through it. Both are reached only from `evict_one`, and both take the key `choose_victim` named, so introducing a new way to *choose* a victim cannot introduce a new way to *remove* one. |
| Outcome variant | `RemovalReason::Evicted` (event + `EvictionKeysTotal`/`EvictionBytesTotal`) / spill (`TieredSpills`/`TieredBytesSpilled`, no event) |
| Forced by | `eviction_replicates_del_and_notifies`, `eviction_is_durable_across_restart`, `spill_emits_no_evicted_notification_but_true_eviction_does`, `spill_preserves_watch_version`, `an_eviction_counts_the_keys_and_the_bytes_it_freed` |
| Bug refs | — |

## FM-MEMORY-007 — eviction frees a key or reports that it cannot; it never spins

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Sustained write pressure against a shard over its limit whose candidate set is empty or too small to get back under it — every key persistent under `volatile-lru`, a warm-tier failure under a tiered policy, or simply a dataset whose live keys exceed `maxmemory`. |
| Observable | The shard keeps serving: writes are refused with `-OOM` and reads are answered from the keys that are still there. The refusal arrives in bounded time, and repeated attempts do not degrade — the pass is bounded whether or not it frees anything. On the segmented backend, the same bound holds inside the keyspace: one victim walk visits each segment a bounded number of times and returns "no candidates" rather than circling the queues, and one call never nominates the same key twice (the caller deletes what it is handed). |
| NOT observable | A hang, a livelock, or an unbounded pass: no input makes the eviction driver or the keyspace's victim walk run for a time that is not bounded by the shard's own size. A pass that reports "freed" without freeing, which would turn the driver's bound into an infinite retry at the caller. Also not observable: a *fair* bound — a pass may give up while the policy still had candidates it did not reach (the driver's ten attempts, the walk's step bound), because the caller's answer to "not enough freed" is a refusal, and a refusal is always a safe answer. |
| Invariant | Two bounds, one per layer. The driver's is `max_attempts = 10` in `check_memory_for_write_inner`, plus `evict_one` returning `false` the moment the policy has no candidate, which exits the loop early rather than retrying. The keyspace's is `Table::cold_candidates`: the walk visits one queue at a time from the tail (coldest), reads each segment's warmer neighbour — its `q_prev` — *before* touching it, and a segment can be moved at most once per epoch (`reconcile` stamps `last_touch`), so `2n + 2` steps is a proven bound and is asserted as one. Within a segment, `nominate_from` stops after one lap of the victim cursor, so the ring cannot re-offer a key inside a single call. Repeated refusals do not re-pay that bound: `TableKeyspace` remembers the `(volatile_only, generation)` of a walk that came back empty and answers "nothing to take" without walking until a mutation bumps `Table::generation` (insert, remove, clear, or the `get_mut` an EXPIRE/PERSIST/unspill changes eligibility through), so a shard refusing writes against an unevictable keyspace costs O(1) per refusal rather than O(segments) — for *consecutive* refusals with no intervening mutation, where a command-path read counts as one (`HashMapStore::get_with_expiry_check` stamps the LRU clock and the LFU counter through `get_mut`), so a read between two refused writes makes the second walk again. A walk that was never made is not evidence either: a `want == 0` request is answered without walking and is not cached. Only an *inert* walk is remembered, and that is a soundness condition rather than a tuning choice: a visit either reconciles a segment or asks it for victims, never both, so a walk that promoted something withheld it from nomination and a repeat may produce what it refused. Promotions and retirements during a walk therefore bump the generation too, and the cache is written only when the generation the walk started with is the one it ended with. Neither bound depends on the clock advancing: a constant `epoch` freezes promotion, never nomination. |
| Outcome variant | `CommandError::OutOfMemory` / `Table::cold_candidates == 0` |
| Forced by | `an_unevictable_keyspace_refuses_writes_and_still_serves_reads`, `a_walk_with_nothing_to_take_reports_zero_rather_than_spinning`, `a_frozen_epoch_still_makes_progress`, `random_reference_and_growth_sequences_keep_the_queues_consistent`, `a_second_refusal_at_an_unchanged_keyspace_does_not_walk_again`, `a_refusal_under_one_confinement_does_not_answer_the_other`, `only_a_possible_change_of_contents_moves_the_generation`, `a_walk_that_promotes_a_segment_moves_the_generation`, `asking_for_no_candidates_does_not_cache_a_refusal` |
| Bug refs | [memory-architecture issue 12](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/done/12-segment-2q-eviction.md) |

## FM-MEMORY-008 — a shard's arena figure is that shard's own bytes, says so before it is taken, and is never read on a shard core

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Any read of the per-shard allocator figures: the sampler's tick, the broker's `arena_sampled_upper_bound_bytes`, and the per-shard rows of the memory breakdown. Also the degenerate configurations — a shard with no arena, a build with no arenas at all, and a registry larger than one tick may read. |
| Observable | A shard's figure covers that shard's own thread and nobody else's: several shard-shaped threads each holding a different known volume each report at least their own bytes and no more than their own bytes plus slack, so a neighbour's allocation cannot appear in this shard's row. A shard the sampler has not reached yet reports **unsampled** rather than zero, and derives no fragmentation ratio from its placeholder zeros; a shard with no arena is absent from the registry rather than present with zeros; an empty registry reports nothing rather than a total of zero. Past `MAX_ARENAS_PER_TICK` a tick reads a contiguous stride and consecutive ticks cover every arena exactly once, so a large registry becomes stale rather than partial. The guard that catches a tick on a shard thread counts `frogdb_arena_sampler_on_shard_thread_total` in every build and fails the process in a debug one. |
| NOT observable | A per-shard figure that is the *process's* memory: the total deliberately excludes the automatic arena, where every non-shard thread allocates, so `INFO memory`'s process-wide fields remain the answer to that question and this figure is never substituted for them. A shard's arena figure driving the `maxmemory` verdict — that binds to accounted contents ([FM-MEMORY-004](#fm-memory-004--eviction-runs-only-under-the-maxmemory-verdict-and-a-write-is-refused-only-after-the-policy-has-been-given-its-chances)); an arena figure is an upper bound on live application bytes and reports what is parked in a thread cache as live. Sampling on a shard core: the tick runs on a utility thread, and thread *affinity* is not what is asserted — a default deployment leaves the sampler's mask unrestricted, so the observable is where the tick is executing, which jemalloc answers because a shard thread is exactly a thread bound to one of the registry's arenas. An epoch advance on a command path: the merge is over every arena, so a request that reached one would pay an allocator-wide operation. A sampler ticking with nothing to sample — a simulation build spawns none. A configured rate honoured outside ADR-0006 §3's 10–100 Hz band, or above what the arena count affords: cost is `hz × arenas × epoch-cost`, so the rate comes down as shards multiply, floored at `MIN_HZ` because a bound more than 100 ms stale is the worse of the two failures. |
| Invariant | `ShardArenaRegistry` is built once from `ShardExecutor::arena_of` after the shards launch, and bindings are fixed for the life of the process — an arena is bound once at shard-thread start and never rebound (ADR-0006 §3), so there is no registration path to race. `ShardArenaRegistry::refresh_stride` is the only caller of `jemalloc::advance_epoch` outside that function's own definition, structurally asserted by scanning the server's crates rather than by inspection. `shard_arena_of_current_thread` is the single detection decision and `assert_off_shard_thread` its single use, counting before it asserts so the release-build surface is the one a debug test exercises. `ArenaSampleRate::for_arena_count` is the only constructor the server uses, and it clamps into the band *and* into the CPU budget; `ArenaSampler::spawn` returns `None` for an empty registry rather than ticking over nothing. |
| Outcome variant | `ShardArenaSample` (`is_sampled() == false` before the first tick) / `ShardArenaRegistry::empty()` (nothing to sample) / `ArenaSamplerOnShardThreadTotal` (a tick on a shard core) |
| Forced by | `each_arena_reports_its_own_shards_bytes_and_no_others`, `the_sampler_makes_a_bound_threads_bytes_visible_per_shard`, `an_empty_registry_reports_nothing_rather_than_zero`, `a_shard_without_an_arena_is_absent_not_zero`, `an_unsampled_slot_says_so_instead_of_reporting_an_empty_shard`, `a_strided_sweep_eventually_samples_every_shard`, `the_guard_passes_on_a_thread_that_is_not_a_shard`, `the_guard_catches_a_tick_running_on_a_shard_thread`, `arena_sampling_is_not_on_a_command_path`, `the_sample_rate_is_budgeted_against_the_arena_count`, `the_sampler_declines_to_run_when_there_is_nothing_to_sample` |
| Bug refs | [memory-architecture issue 03](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/done/03-arena-binding-and-sampled-stats.md), [issue 07](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/done/07-wire-arena-registry-into-broker.md), [issue 08](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/done/08-arena-bind-fail-fast.md), [issue 20](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/done/20-fragmentation-polish-purge-decay-metrics.md) |

## What the simulation cannot force

**After the thread-per-core move, turmoil tests production logic, not production execution
shape.** A shard is an OS thread with a pinned runtime and a bound arena; the
shard-placement seam has a simulation implementation that multiplexes every shard back
onto the one sim thread and makes arena binding a no-op, because a shard on its own thread
escapes the simulation's scheduler and virtual clock and takes determinism with it. The
seam is what keeps the existing suite alive across the change (see
[spike-report.md](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/spike-report.md) §(c)).

The consequence for this spec is a rule about forcing tests, and every row above is subject
to it. **A row whose behavior depends on any of the following may not name a turmoil test as
its forcing test**, and must name a real-thread harness instead:

1. **Allocator behavior.** Per-arena statistics, fragmentation ratios, per-shard `maxmemory`
   verdicts, and eviction driven by allocator truth do not exist under simulation — every
   shard allocates from one thread's arena there.
2. **Real memory-ordering effects.** The simulation serializes everything onto one thread,
   so it cannot exhibit a race between two shard threads, a torn read, or false sharing.
   Those belong to the shuttle/loom-style tools the workspace already carries.
3. **Cross-core cost.** A cross-core hop is free in the simulation and roughly 8× a
   same-core request in reality. No performance claim is ever forced by a sim test.
4. **The absence of foreign-thread frees.** The no-cross-arena-bleed rule is trivially true
   under a single thread and therefore untested there; it needs a real-thread assertion —
   which is why FM-MEMORY-008's `each_arena_reports_its_own_shards_bytes_and_no_others`
   spawns real threads.

What *is* preserved under simulation, and may be forced there: message ordering between
shards and connections, network latency and partitions, virtual time, the totally ordered
per-shard command queue, and every protocol- and consistency-level invariant the existing
simulations already assert. All of those are properties of the shard body, which is shared
code across both implementations of the seam.

## Open items

Scope this spec claims and does not yet contract. Each is a gap with a filed issue, not a
promise the rows may be read as covering — a locked spec describes what exists.

* **"Every buffer is bounded and budget-charged" is not yet true.** The load-bearing claim
  of the area — *a structure that cannot charge cannot grow* — has its chokepoint (the
  `lint-budget-growth` seam lint, [`agents/seam-lints.md`](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/agents/seam-lints.md)) and its
  ratchet, but the allowlist still pins **83 unconverted growth sites across 32 files**
  against 20 budgeted ones. Three declared subsystems (`replication_backlog`,
  `wal_channel`, `fullsync_staging`) are charged by nobody. Until the allowlist is empty
  there is no row here claiming a buffer is bounded that does not name its own `Budget`.
  [Issue 24](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/open/24-budget-growth-allowlist-burndown.md).
* **There is no snapshot handle.** A *snapshot handle* would be a reference to a value taken
  for reading while writers continue — pointer work, not a copy, with a subsequent write
  copying rather than mutating what the handle sees — bounding an export's memory to what it
  has not yet streamed, as the in-process substitute for Redis's fork (PRD R6). What exists
  today is record-level refcount copy-on-write inside the table, which is not that contract:
  a full sync still materializes. Full-sync double materialization is a known cost, not a
  specified impossibility. [Issue 25](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/open/25-snapshot-handle-bounded-full-sync.md).
* **The replication receive path holds a ceiling, not a budget.**
  [replication.md FM-REPLICATION-068](/specifications/replication/#fm-replication-068--a-live-dataset-blob-is-bounded-before-it-is-allocated-and-read-a-chunk-at-a-time)
  bounds a wire-supplied dataset blob against a 16 GiB constant before allocating, and says
  so itself: *"A ceiling is not a budget."* It defends against one absurd claim; it does not
  size the receive against the node's actual memory. When that path holds a `Budget` the
  constant stays as the cheap early refusal and a row here takes over the question the
  ceiling never answered — a row plus an amendment there, not a deletion.
  [Issue 26](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/open/26-replication-receive-budget.md).
* **The replica-feed hold buffer has no byte cap.**
  [cluster.md TR-CLUSTER-016](/specifications/cluster/#tr-cluster-016--replica-feed-hold-during-an-armed-slot-barrier)
  rules one and the code does not have it. It is deliberately not being implemented against
  the current row (the cluster campaign is rewriting that row to ordinary replica-feed
  backpressure), so it lands here once that rewrite settles.
  [Issue 27](https://github.com/frogdb/frogdb/blob/main/.scratch/memory-architecture/issues/open/27-replica-feed-hold-byte-cap.md).

[persistence.md](/specifications/persistence/) owns durability ordering and the write-group atomicity the
transaction-buffer cap bounds. [replication.md](/specifications/replication/) owns what crosses the link;
this spec owns what holding it costs. [cluster.md](/specifications/cluster/) owns slot ownership; this
spec owns what a cross-slot hop copies and who is charged for the copy.
[blocking.md](/specifications/blocking/) owns the parked-wait contract, including the parked pipeline
buffer FM-MEMORY-003 keeps from pinning a read buffer.
